query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Grain boundary morphology governs toughness degradation in single-phase HEAs; specifically, straight GBs induce localized strain concentration and brittle intergranular fracture, while inducing serration enhances ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase HEA (e.g., a precipitation-strengthened variant) fabricated under rapid cooling conditions that yield predominantly straight grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Apply a tailored heat treatment with a controlled slow cooling rate to induce serrated grain boundary morphologies without altering the overall composition.
generation.conditions: Heat treat in an inert atmosphere at elevated temperatures followed by varied cooling rates to produce samples with straight versus serrated GBs; mechanical testing at ~650°C.
generation.structural_mediator: Distinct grain boundary morphologies: straight (baseline) versus serrated (engineered) as verified by TEM/EBSD.
generation.mechanism: Serrated grain boundaries facilitate a more uniform strain distribution and impede intergranular crack propagation, whereas straight boundaries concentrate strain at triple junctions, predisposing the material to brittle failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with engineered serrated GBs will display significantly higher tensile ductility and prolonged creep rupture life, along with transgranular-dominant fracture, compared to samples with straight GBs.
generation.baseline: HEA samples processed with rapid cooling that produce straight grain boundaries and are prone to brittle intergranular fracture under high-temperature loading.
generation.boundary: Relevant for high-temperature applications (around 650°C) under both tensile and creep loading conditions.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative control and reproducibility of GB serration amplitude and its direct correlation with toughness improvements require further calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Process identical HEA samples with controlled cooling rates to produce two groups with distinct GB morphologies (straight versus serrated). Perform tensile and creep tests at 650°C and analyze GB strain distribution via EBSD.
measurements: Tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples with serrated GBs do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in ductility and creep performance, or if strain distribution remains similar to that in straight GB samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Both HT-1 and HT-2 samples have almost identical tensile strength and ductility at 25°C (Table 1 and Figure 6); ductile transgranular fractures were dominant at room temperature (Figure 7(a,c)). However, when testing temperature was increased to 650°C, a significant hot ductility drop was observed for HT-1 sample. According to Figure 7(b), the facet cleavage surface and the limited amount of plastic deformation indicate that the failure mechanism was brittle intergranular fracture. The brittleness of HT-1 sample was even more pronounced under creep at 650°C as the creep fracture strain was only 0.03%. Cleavage edges on crept fracture surface (Figure 9(b)) and crack propagation along straight grain boundary (Figure 10(b)) indicate the vulnerability of straight grain boundary in HT-1 samples at elevated temperature. According to the local strain concentration at triple junctions of grain boundaries (Figure 11(a)), it is probable that HT-1 samples encountered an embrittlement at 650°C. The initiation of creep damage of HT-1 sample was a result of vacancy coalescence on grain boundaries perpendicular to the loading direction and severe strain concentration at grain boundaries. The effect of serrated grain boundary on tensile and creep properties has been investigated for a high-entropy alloy (Al8Co35Cr18Ni34Ti3Nb2Zr0.005B0.01 (at.%)) fabricated by selective laser melting, the followings are findings of this work: Serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. The inferior ductility of straight grain boundary at 650°C was attributed to the grain boundary embrittlement caused by strain concentration at triple junctions and fast intergranular crack propagation. The slow cooling process of the post heat treatment could coarsen the γ′ particles and encourage interactions with mobile grain boundaries to from serrated grain boundaries. Analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology. Serrated grain boundaries could reduce local strain concentration and provide resistance against intergranular cracking.

papers.title: Deformation-induced grain boundary segregation in a powder-metallurgy ultrafine-grained MoNbTaTiV refractory high-entropy alloy.
papers.approach: Powder metallurgy synthesis (mechanical alloying, spark plasma sintering) followed by hot deformation at varied temperatures and strain rates to induce segregation
papers.findings: At relatively low deformation temperatures and high strain rates, significant component element segregation near grain boundaries is observed; increasing the temperature and lowering the strain rate gradually eliminates segregation. Segregation leads to localized microhardness variations.
papers.mechanism: Dislocation movement and associated slip (plus defect generation) under plastic deformation drive the migration and accumulation of multi‐principal elements at grain boundaries.

papers.title: Grain boundary decohesion by nanoclustering Ni and Cr separately in CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys.
papers.approach: Tensile testing at intermediate temperatures with atom probe tomography analysis to detect the nanoclustering behavior of principal elements
papers.findings: Ductility loss at intermediate temperatures is correlated with the nanoclustering of Ni, Cr, and Mn at grain boundaries, which reduces grain boundary cohesion and promotes intergranular cracking; additionally, a strategy utilizing preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases can migrate the fast segregation away from the boundaries.
papers.mechanism: Fast, temperature-activated nanosegregation of principal alloying elements leads to localized grain boundary decohesion, initiating intergranular fracture in an otherwise single-phase material.

papers.title: Mitigating Strain Localization via Stabilized Phase Boundaries for Strengthening Multi-Principal Element Alloys.
papers.system: Multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) with engineered dual-phase (enamel-like) microstructure
papers.approach: Microstructure design that stabilizes nanoscale phase boundaries to provide ample plastic space for dislocation transfer and to mitigate strain localization
papers.findings: The stabilized phase boundaries effectively dissipate local strain, enabling ultra-high tensile strength along with good ductility, through mechanisms such as crack deflection, blocking, and bridging.
papers.mechanism: The introduction and stabilization of dual-phase (BCC and FCC) regions create phase boundaries that act as pathways for trans-phase dislocation migration, reducing localized strain and mitigating premature failure.

papers.title: Effect of serrated grain boundary on tensile and creep properties of a precipitation strengthened high entropy alloy.
papers.system: Precipitation-strengthened high-entropy alloy fabricated by selective laser melting
papers.approach: Tailoring the grain boundary (GB) morphology via controlled cooling and heat treatment to transform straight GBs into serrated ones
papers.findings: At elevated temperatures (around 650°C), alloys with serrated GBs show significantly improved tensile fracture strain and enhanced creep rupture life compared to those with straight GBs; serrated boundaries distribute strain more evenly and delay intergranular crack propagation.
papers.mechanism: The serrated GB morphology reduces local strain concentration—especially at triple junctions—thereby retarding intergranular crack propagation and mitigating brittle failure at high temperature.

papers.title: Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of Intergranular Boride Precipitation-Toughened HfMoNbTaTiZr Refractory High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: Refractory HEA (HfMoNbTaTiZr) with minor boron addition
papers.approach: Alloy design incorporating a small amount of boron to prompt intergranular precipitation of borides via controlled processing
papers.findings: The presence of intergranular boride precipitates markedly increases the hardness and cohesion of grain boundaries, leading to improved work hardenability and ductility with a shift from predominantly intergranular to transgranular fracture modes.
papers.mechanism: Minor boron addition induces precipitation of (Hf, Zr)B2 borides at the grain boundaries, reinforcing these regions and preventing decohesion that would otherwise lead to brittle fracture.

established: In conventional alloys, toughness degradation is often linked with grain-boundary segregation and brittle intermetallic precipitation.
High-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and intermetallic formation, thereby exhibiting favorable strength–ductility combinations.
Under deformation, multi-principal element systems exhibit unique grain boundary segregation behavior that can both enhance and degrade mechanical properties.

approaches_tried.approach: Deformation-induced grain boundary segregation via controlled hot deformation (varying temperature and strain rate)
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated that mechanical processing conditions directly influence the extent of elemental segregation at grain boundaries; lower temperatures/high strain rates promote segregation, which may degrade toughness.

approaches_tried.approach: GB segregation engineering using preexisting Cr-rich precipitates to absorb embrittling elements
approaches_tried.outcome: Found effective in mitigating ductility loss at intermediate temperatures by shifting fast segregation from grain boundaries to secondary phases.

approaches_tried.approach: Microstructure design via stabilized phase boundaries (enamel-like dual-phase mixtures)
approaches_tried.outcome: Reduced strain localization and enhanced both tensile strength and ductility in MPEAs.

approaches_tried.approach: Tailoring grain boundary morphology from straight to serrated through heat treatment control
approaches_tried.outcome: Serrated grain boundaries significantly improve high-temperature ductility and creep resistance by alleviating local strain concentrations.

approaches_tried.approach: Addition of minor alloying elements (boron) to induce intergranular boride precipitation
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced grain boundary cohesion and ductility, shifting failure from intergranular to transgranular modes.

mechanisms: Dislocation-mediated migration of multi-principal elements leading to segregation at grain boundaries.
Nanoclustering of principal alloying elements (e.g., Ni, Cr, Mn) that reduces grain boundary cohesion.
Stabilized phase boundaries that accommodate dislocation transfer and mitigate localized strain concentration.
Grain boundary morphological effects (serration) that distribute strain more evenly and delay crack propagation.
Intergranular precipitation (e.g., borides) that reinforces grain boundaries and prevents decohesion.
disagreements: The role of grain refinement in HEAs is debated: while it can reduce segregation levels in conventional alloys, in HEAs it may promote segregation of principal elements and formation of brittle phases.
There is discussion over whether the brittleness originates solely from conventional intermetallic formation or from unique nanosegregation phenomena specific to multi-principal element systems.
The relative impact of dislocation dynamics versus static phase boundary morphology on preventing toughness degradation remains under debate.
open_questions: What is the precise threshold at which deformation-induced grain boundary segregation in single-phase HEAs transitions from beneficial strengthening to detrimental embrittlement?
How do service conditions (loading rate, temperature) interact with the intrinsic segregation tendencies of multi-principal elements to trigger brittle behavior?
Can a controlled comparison be devised to clearly separate the effects of grain boundary decohesion due to nanoclustering from those due to conventional embrittlement mechanisms?
What is the quantitative relationship between the degree of segregation (or GB morphology modification) and the resulting changes in toughness in a single-phase HEA?
opportunities: Perform controlled experiments on a single-phase HEA where deformation temperature and strain rate are systematically varied to map the onset of nanosegregation-induced brittleness versus stable behavior.
Combine GB segregation engineering (e.g., introducing preexisting secondary phases) with grain boundary morphology control (serration) to study synergistic effects on toughness.
Utilize in situ microscopy (e.g., TEM with in situ straining) coupled with atom probe tomography to correlate dislocation dynamics and nanoclustering at GBs.

Investigate the role of minor alloying additions (like boron) in different compositionally complex systems to extend the strategy of intergranular strengthening with minimal compromise to phase complexity.

Develop predictive models to link processing conditions, segregation kinetics, and mechanical performance in high-entropy alloys, thereby guiding the design of compositionally complex systems with retained ductility at service conditions.

directions.direction: Investigate deformation‐induced nanosegregation of the principal elements at grain boundaries under varied strain rates and temperatures.
directions.assessment: Directly targets the unique dislocation-driven segregation in HEAs as opposed to conventional trace-element segregation. Well supported by evidence from deformation studies (e.g., PMC11407990, PMC6897545). Feasible with current atom probe and TEM techniques.

directions.direction: Examine thermally activated diffusion leading to subtle nanocluster formation at grain boundaries during post-deformation annealing.
directions.assessment: Addresses potential service-related toughness degradation due to time-temperature dependent segregation phenomena. Evidence suggests that even in single-phase HEAs, thermal exposure can trigger nanoclustering (PMC6897545). Feasible via controlled annealing experiments.

directions.direction: Control the grain boundary morphology (straight vs. serrated) via tailored heat treatments.
directions.assessment: Distinguishes how GB shape, not just chemistry, effects toughness. Prior studies (e.g., PMC9848264) show serrated boundaries mitigate strain localization, offering a controlled comparison with conventional expectations.

directions.direction: Employ minor alloying additions (e.g., boron) to induce beneficial intergranular precipitation that reinforces grain boundaries.
directions.assessment: Transforms a potential vulnerability—GB segregation—into a reinforcing mechanism. Prior evidence (e.g., PMC9572892) supports GB strengthening via boride precipitation in HEAs while retaining phase complexity.

directions.direction: Study the role of twin boundary network formation and its evolution under service loading on toughness.
directions.assessment: Although promising, the role of 3D twinning in affecting toughness is more complex; while it contributes to strengthening, its direct link to brittle behavior is less clear relative to GB effects. More challenging to decouple from other mechanisms.

candidates.hypothesis: High strain rate and lower temperature deformation in a single-phase HEA triggers dislocation-mediated nanosegregation of principal elements to grain boundaries, reducing cohesion and causing brittle failure.
candidates.intervention: Subject samples to controlled hot deformation with a high strain rate (e.g., >10⁻³ s⁻¹) at lower/intermediate temperatures versus a condition with higher temperature and lower strain rate.

candidates.hypothesis: At service-relevant intermediate temperatures, thermally activated diffusion in a single-phase HEA drives the nanoclustering of principal elements at grain boundaries, transitioning the fracture mode from ductile transgranular to brittle intergranular.
candidates.intervention: Expose samples to post-deformation thermal annealing at intermediate temperatures.

candidates.hypothesis: Grain boundary morphology governs toughness degradation in single-phase HEAs; specifically, straight GBs induce localized strain concentration and brittle intergranular fracture, while inducing serration enhances ductility.
candidates.intervention: Apply a tailored heat treatment with a controlled slow cooling rate to induce serrated grain boundary morphologies without altering the overall composition.

candidates.hypothesis: Minor alloying with boron in a single-phase HEA promotes in-situ intergranular boride precipitation that reinforces GB cohesion and prevents the onset of brittle behavior.
candidates.intervention: Introduce a minor boron addition (approximately 0.1 at.%) during synthesis to trigger the precipitation of (Hf, Zr)B₂ borides preferentially at grain boundaries.
